desc:
The m x n matrix grid contains only 0 and 1. Inside every row, all the zeros come before all the ones (each row is sorted in non-decreasing order).

Return the 0-based index of the row that contains the most ones. If several rows tie, return the smallest index. If the matrix contains no 1 at all, return -1.

Counting every cell takes O(m * n); try to finish in O(m + n).
constraints: Each row is in non-decreasing order
hints: Because each row is sorted, the number of ones in a row is decided by where its first 1 sits. A binary search per row finds it in O(log n).

You do not need the exact count of every row, only to know whether a row beats the best one so far. Suppose the best row so far has its first 1 at column c; a new row beats it only if it has a 1 at column c - 1.

Start at the top-right corner with col = n - 1. For each row, keep moving left while the cell is 1; if you moved at all, this row is the new best. The column pointer never moves right, so the whole scan is O(m + n).
editorial: The simple solutions are to count the ones in each row (O(m * n)) or to binary search the first 1 of each row (O(m log n)). The sortedness of rows allows something better.

Keep a pointer col, initially n - 1, that marks the leftmost column where some row seen so far has a 1 (all columns before it are either unseen or hold zero in the best row). For the next row, slide col left while grid[row][col] == 1. If the pointer moved, this row has strictly more ones than any earlier row, so it becomes the best. If it did not move, the row has at most as many ones as the best row, and since ties keep the earlier row, nothing changes.

The pointer only decreases and the row index only increases, so there are at most m + n steps: O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space. If the pointer never moved, no row contained a one and the answer is -1.
